raw_evidence.label: Doritos 'Crash the Super Bowl' — 36,000+ fan-made ad submissions
raw_evidence.content: From 2006 to 2016, Doritos ran an open contest called 'Crash the Super Bowl': anyone could submit a 30-second ad, and the winning entries actually aired during the game. Across eight editions, fans submitted more than 36,000 entries. The first ever crowdsourced spot, 'Live the Flavor' (2007), placed #4 on the Ad Meter; in 2009 the fan-made 'Free Doritos' won the entire Ad Meter. Every Crash ad that aired finished in the Ad Meter top five. This explains a small mystery in the data: Doritos has 25 spots in 21 years — more than any non-Anheuser brand — and the Doritos run is also why the dataset has so many high-view-count amateur-styled clips.

sources.title: Crash the Super Bowl — Wikipedia
facts: Run from 2006 to 2016 in eight editions

21 Crash ads aired during the game; all finished in Ad Meter top 5
'Live the Flavor' (2007) was the first ever crowdsourced ad to air; placed #4 on the USA Today Ad Meter
'Free Doritos' (2009) won the Ad Meter outright

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters — Super Bowl ads are the single biggest culture-vs-money artifact
raw_evidence.content: The Super Bowl draws around 100 million U.S. viewers a year, the only TV event with consistently that kind of reach in a streaming era. A 30-second spot now costs eight figures in production plus seven figures in airtime, and it has to compete with the game itself for attention. So Super Bowl creative is the most expensive and most public laboratory we have for what advertisers think will move humans en masse. When the trait mix shifts — when 'use sex' falls and 'patriotic' rises — that shift is not just creative drift, it is a cultural pulse-check that the brands are paying ten million dollars apiece to take.

raw_evidence.label: Top-viewed ads — Doritos Sling Baby (2012) leads at 176 million YouTube views
raw_evidence.content: Sorted by YouTube view_count, the top ad is Doritos Sling Baby (2012, 176.4 million views) — a Crash the Super Bowl winner. Second is Budweiser's 'Born The Hard Way' (2017, 28.8 million), which traces Adolphus Busch's immigration from Germany. Third is the NFL's 'Next 100' (2020, 26.7 million). The gap is gigantic: rank #1 has 6x the views of rank #2, and the median ad in the dataset has just 41,379 views. View counts on Super Bowl ads are extremely fat-tailed.

raw_evidence.label: FiveThirtyEight watched 233 ads from the 10 most-prolific brands
raw_evidence.content: The dataset comes from FiveThirtyEight, which in early 2021 published 'According to Super Bowl Ads, Americans Love America (and Animals).' Their team watched 233 commercials from the 10 brands that aired the most spots in the 21 Super Bowls of this century, all sourced from superbowl-ads.com. They evaluated each spot on seven yes/no defining criteria: funny, shows the product quickly, patriotic, features a celebrity, contains danger, contains animals, and uses sex. The TidyTuesday distribution joined these tags to YouTube metadata (view counts, likes, channel, publish date) for 247 rows, with 14 rows added for repeat uploads of the same commercial.

raw_evidence.label: Why the seven traits matter — they are the agency vocabulary of the genre
raw_evidence.content: FiveThirtyEight's seven traits are not arbitrary. They map almost exactly onto the levers ad agencies talk about when pitching a Super Bowl spot: comedic register (funny), commercial intent (show product quickly), cultural posture (patriotic), star power (celebrity), spectacle (danger), warmth/cuteness (animals), and provocation (use sex). When you see how often each trait shows up across 21 years, you are essentially watching agency taste change in slow motion: the use-sex trait rises and then falls, patriotic spikes after 9/11, animals stay stubbornly common because the Bud Light playbook works.

raw_evidence.label: Trait stacking — only 2 ads check all 7, only 4 check none
raw_evidence.content: The mean Super Bowl ad here checks 2.75 of the seven boxes, and the median is 3. The distribution is hump-shaped: 30.7% have exactly three traits, 26.6% have two, 19.7% have four. Only four ads (1.6%) hit zero traits — they are pure non-funny, no-celebrity, no-animals exposition. At the other end, 17 ads (7.0%) carry five or more traits; just one ad checks six and one checks all seven. The Super Bowl ad recipe, in other words, is a small handful of ingredients combined.

raw_evidence.label: The Budweiser Frogs (1995) — the prototype for the modern Bud playbook
raw_evidence.content: In Super Bowl XXIX (1995), Budweiser aired three swamp puppets named Bud, Weis, and Er croaking the brand name. Directed by Gore Verbinski (later Pirates of the Caribbean), the spot was named one of the most iconic alcohol ads in history. A 1996 study found more children recognized the Budweiser frogs as a beer mascot than recognized Smokey Bear or Tony the Tiger. Although the dataset starts at 2000 — five years after the frogs — the success of that single 30 seconds is part of why Bud Light and Budweiser dominate the volume of ads in the dataset (63 and 43 spots respectively): the frogs proved that an animal-led, dialogue-light comedy can carry a brand year after year.

raw_evidence.label: Doritos 'Crash the Super Bowl' — 36,000+ fan-made ad submissions
raw_evidence.content: From 2006 to 2016, Doritos ran an open contest called 'Crash the Super Bowl': anyone could submit a 30-second ad, and the winning entries actually aired during the game. Across eight editions, fans submitted more than 36,000 entries. The first ever crowdsourced spot, 'Live the Flavor' (2007), placed #4 on the Ad Meter; in 2009 the fan-made 'Free Doritos' won the entire Ad Meter. Every Crash ad that aired finished in the Ad Meter top five. This explains a small mystery in the data: Doritos has 25 spots in 21 years — more than any non-Anheuser brand — and the Doritos run is also why the dataset has so many high-view-count amateur-styled clips.

Source: Breaking Down the Super Bowl Ad Playbook — Darden Report (https://news.darden.virginia.edu/2025/02/10/breaking-down-the-super-bowl-ad-play) Facts: Industry observers describe Super Bowl ads in terms of comedic, emotional, celebrity-led, and patriotic registers — the same axes FiveThirtyEight chose

raw_evidence.label: Why the seven traits matter — they are the agency vocabulary of the genre
raw_evidence.content: FiveThirtyEight's seven traits are not arbitrary. They map almost exactly onto the levers ad agencies talk about when pitching a Super Bowl spot: comedic register (funny), commercial intent (show product quickly), cultural posture (patriotic), star power (celebrity), spectacle (danger), warmth/cuteness (animals), and provocation (use sex). When you see how often each trait shows up across 21 years, you are essentially watching agency taste change in slow motion: the use-sex trait rises and then falls, patriotic spikes after 9/11, animals stay stubbornly common because the Bud Light playbook works.

raw_evidence.label: Era comparison — funny down 27 pp, patriotic up 13 pp
raw_evidence.content: Cut the dataset in half — 2000-2009 versus 2010-2020 — and the change is unmistakable. Funny ads drop from 83.8% of all spots to 56.4%, a 27.4-percentage-point fall. Use_sex falls from 33.3% to 19.5%, down 13.8 pp. Danger declines 8.0 pp. Going the other way: patriotic climbs from 9.9% to 22.6%, +12.7 pp; celebrity climbs from 23.4% to 31.6%, +8.2 pp; animals tick up modestly. The Super Bowl ad of the 2010s is more sober, more star-studded, and more flag-forward than the Super Bowl ad of the 2000s.

raw_evidence.label: Use-sex collapse — 39% in early 2000s, 7% by late 2010s
raw_evidence.content: The cleanest single-trait trend in the dataset is the disappearance of sexual appeals. In 2000-2004, 38.9% of ads from these ten brands used sex to sell. By 2016-2020, that share had fallen to 7.1% — a drop of 31.7 percentage points, an 82% relative decline. The trait went to literal 0% in both 2017 and 2020. Whether you read it as a #MeToo correction, an audience-shift, or a quiet retreat to safer comedy, this is the largest behavior change visible in the data.
raw_evidence.code:
print(f"  {int(y)}: {v}%")
e1 = ads[ads['year'] <= 2004]['use_sex'].mean() * 100
e2 = ads[ads['year'] >= 2016]['use_sex'].mean() * 100
print(f"\n2000-2004: {e1:.1f}% used sex")
print(f"2016-2020: {e2:.1f}% used sex")
print(f"Drop: {e1-e2:.1f} percentage points (~{(e1-e2)/e1*100:.0f}% relative decline)")
print()

# --- ana_10: Most-viewed ad in the dataset ---
print("=== ana_10 ===")

for i, (_, r) in enumerate(ranked.head(10).iterrows(), 1):
    traits_on = [t for t in TRAITS if r[t]]
    print(f"  {i:>2d}. {int(r['year'])} {r['brand']:<14s} {int(r['view_count']):>11,d}  {str(r['title'])[:55]}")
    print(f"      traits: {','.join(traits_on) or '(none)'}  id={r['id']}")
print()

raw_evidence.label: Patriotic spike was 2017, not post-9/11 — counter to expectation
raw_evidence.content: If you guess the patriotic ad spike, you guess 2002 — the first Super Bowl after 9/11. The data says otherwise. Patriotic ads were just 4.8% of these brands' spots in 2000-2001 and only 6.1% in 2002-2004. The actual peak is 2017-2018: 60% of 2017's ads were patriotic (the highest single-year share in the data), 35.7% in 2018. The 2017-2018 window has a 42.1% patriotic rate — the highest two-year window in 21 years. This is the year of Budweiser's 'Born The Hard Way' (immigration story) and a wave of brands explicitly invoking American identity during the early Trump era.

    flag = ''
    if int(y) in (2002, 2003):

    if int(y) in (2017, 2018):
        flag = ' <- Trump-era patriotism wave'
    print(f"  {int(y)}: {v}%{flag}")
print()

pre = ads[ads['year'].isin([2000, 2001])]['patriotic'].mean() * 100

print(f"\n2000-2001 (pre 9/11): {pre:.1f}% patriotic")
print(f"2002-2004 (post 9/11): {post:.1f}% patriotic")
print()

late = ads[ads['year'].isin([2017, 2018])]['patriotic'].mean() * 100

raw_evidence.label: Why the seven traits matter — they are the agency vocabulary of the genre
raw_evidence.content: FiveThirtyEight's seven traits are not arbitrary. They map almost exactly onto the levers ad agencies talk about when pitching a Super Bowl spot: comedic register (funny), commercial intent (show product quickly), cultural posture (patriotic), star power (celebrity), spectacle (danger), warmth/cuteness (animals), and provocation (use sex). When you see how often each trait shows up across 21 years, you are essentially watching agency taste change in slow motion: the use-sex trait rises and then falls, patriotic spikes after 9/11, animals stay stubbornly common because the Bud Light playbook works.

raw_evidence.label: Funny vs patriotic — the strongest negative correlation in the data
raw_evidence.content: Of all 21 trait pairs, the strongest negative correlation is funny vs patriotic at phi = -0.384. Patriotic ads are about 30 percentage points less likely to be funny than non-patriotic ads. The next strongest negatives are celebrity vs animals (-0.186) and patriotic vs danger (-0.157). Among positives, the largest pairs are funny + danger (+0.275) and funny + use_sex (+0.275). Translation: in this dataset, comedy and country-loving rarely sit in the same 30 seconds, and the Super Bowl rules of provocation apply to both edge and skin.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_16: Trait pairwise correlations (phi coefficient = pearson on 0/1) ---
print("=== ana_16 ===")
trait_df = ads[TRAITS].astype(int)
corr = trait_df.corr().round(3)
print("Pairwise phi correlation (rows vs cols):")
print(corr.to_string())
print()
# Find strongest +/- correlations
pairs = []
cols = TRAITS
for i, a in enumerate(cols):
    for b in cols[i+1:]:
        pairs.append((a, b, corr.loc[a, b]))
pairs.sort(key=lambda x: x[2])
print("\nMost negative trait pairs:")
for a, b, c in pairs[:5]:
    print(f"  {a:25s} vs {b:25s}: {c:+.3f}")
print("\nMost positive trait pairs:")
for a, b, c in sorted(pairs, key=lambda x: -x[2])[:5]:

raw_evidence.label: Super Bowl 30-second ad price more than doubled, 2000 to 2020
raw_evidence.content: A 30-second slot during Super Bowl XXXIV in 2000 cost about $2.1-$2.2 million. By Super Bowl LIV in 2020 it had climbed to roughly $5.4 million. The price crossed $3 million in 2011, $4 million in 2014, and $5 million in 2017. So the 21 years in this dataset are also a doubling-and-then-some of the cost-per-second floor, which sharpens the question of whether the creative formula changed in step.

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters — Super Bowl ads are the single biggest culture-vs-money artifact
raw_evidence.content: The Super Bowl draws around 100 million U.S. viewers a year, the only TV event with consistently that kind of reach in a streaming era. A 30-second spot now costs eight figures in production plus seven figures in airtime, and it has to compete with the game itself for attention. So Super Bowl creative is the most expensive and most public laboratory we have for what advertisers think will move humans en masse. When the trait mix shifts — when 'use sex' falls and 'patriotic' rises — that shift is not just creative drift, it is a cultural pulse-check that the brands are paying ten million dollars apiece to take.

raw_evidence.content: Of the 128 distinct trait combinations in the data, the most common is the bare 'funny + show product quickly' pair (23 ads, 9.4%). Next most common: 'funny + show product quickly + danger' (15 ads), 'show product quickly only' (11), and the four-trait recipe 'funny + show product quickly + danger + animals' (11). Each of the next eight combinations appears 6-10 times. The genre, in other words, is built from a small number of repeated formulas — and the most popular formula is the simplest one.

n = len(bl)

print(f"Bud Light: {n} ads")
print(f"  funny:           {funny_pct:.1f}%")
print(f"  show product fast: {fast_pct:.1f}%")
print(f"  BOTH funny + fast:  {both_pct:.1f}%")
neither = ((~bl['funny']) & (~bl['show_product_quickly'])).mean() * 100

print()

raw_evidence.content: The Super Bowl draws around 100 million U.S. viewers a year, the only TV event with consistently that kind of reach in a streaming era.
